### 4. Finding the Right Fit ###

#### Choosing a System for the Experience I Want ####

For me, the system is almost inconsequential. You can tell any kind of story with any kind of system. What matters most is that the table will have fun with the system; everything after that can be patched.

That does not mean system choice is meaningless. I recommend that GMs understand what they like and dislike. I personally don't run tactical systems anymore because I don't find them fun. I prefer story-based systems, so I tend to run games such as World of Darkness, Fate, and Cypher. Those are my tastes, not a universal recommendation. Choose a system the table wants to play, then adapt what needs adapting.

#### Finding Players Who Want That Experience ####

I am up front with players about the kind of game I expect to run. I may not reveal the exact theme if doing so would give too much away, but I talk about what kinds of things will be in the story and what parts of play are likely to take focus: combat, narrative, investigation, or some combination.

I also tell players what topics I want to address, especially when those topics might be trigger topics. Players need enough information to decide whether they want to join, even when some details of the story remain a surprise.

#### Establishing Expectations, Boundaries, and Feedback ####

Safety is the ultimate authority at my table. We decide together what can initially go into the game and when it can happen. Every player can veto content at any time, no questions asked. If a veto is used, I remove the offending context, make a note, and after the session ask only whether I recorded it correctly so it can be added to our banned-topics list.

I don't start a game with a player until we have practiced vetoing topics twice. The first practice is usually silly: I might say, “Ham is your trigger topic and bread is yours,” then describe a scene that includes one of those topics so everyone can try using a veto. I repeat the exercise with a different, real example, such as animal abuse, if it is not already on the forbidden-topics list.

The practices help make vetoing an available action before a real boundary is tested in play. A veto does not require explanation. If the veto concerns an action by a player character, I work with that player to find another action the character can take.

### 5. Creating a Starting Point ###

#### What I Need to Know Before Play Begins ####

I think of campaign creation as building a physics engine. I create a situation with forces that can move the world, then let the characters enter it and change what happens. I need to understand that situation well enough to respond when the players surprise me. I do not need to know what story they will produce.

Three constructs help me do this: forces, the Stage, and Arcs. Forces pursue goals. The Stage gives those forces a world to act in. Collisions between their actions start Arcs, whose events develop through play.

##### Forces #####

Power alone does not make someone a force. A force must have all four of these qualities:

- It is more powerful than the characters.
- It has a goal it is trying to achieve.
- It has lines it will and will not cross.
- It has a fingerprint: findable evidence that lets the players recognize separate actions as the work of the same person or group.

What counts as more powerful depends on the campaign and what I want to emphasize. A fingerprint might be a method, a trace left behind, or a way of treating people. It can be deliberate or incidental. A force can be an individual or a group; I can treat a group as one character for its shared goal while still treating its members as individuals.

I also create supporting characters. They do not need to meet the criteria for a force. They can connect the characters to forces, show the effects of those forces, or carry a thematic or emotional thread of their own.

As a rule of thumb, I start with three forces. I give them goals that do not directly oppose one another. Their ways of pursuing those goals can bring them into conflict, but their purposes do not need to be opposite sides of the same struggle.

For my purposes, directly opposing goals simplify two forces down to a single force: everything they do interacts. Separate goals give me more possibilities for the conflicts they generate.

##### The Stage #####

The Stage is the background of the campaign: its props, places, stories, and relationships. It explains why the forces I have chosen are the forces that matter here. It also needs enough life and movement that other forces can emerge.

Most games already have a canon that describes a populated world. That is usually my starting place, not something I need to replace. My Stage describes some portion of that world and adds enough depth that it feels alive.

I map relationships between forces, including alliances, rivalries, obligations, history, and dependencies. I consider how people and local groups view them: who loves a force, who hates it, and who would hate it if they knew its identity. I distinguish what people know from what they believe, including what the forces know or believe about one another. These notes can be light; a sentence or three may be enough to give me something useful.

The Stage and forces develop together. A force gives me reasons to build parts of the Stage, and those parts suggest new forces. Often I begin play with different forces from the ones that originally inspired me because better options emerge during development. Neither exists independently of the other.

In the campaign with the Nephondi High Mage, he was the initial force. I needed a Stage that allowed him to exist and pursue his goal. That led to the spirit beneath the city. Once I had the spirit, I realized I needed guardians. Because the campaign was set in Baton Rouge, that development led to a were-gator tribe becoming another force.

This connected work is where most of my initial development goes. I may produce dozens of ideas for possible forces, but that is a side effect. I only need three to begin.

##### When the Stage Is Ready #####

I use four criteria to decide when I have developed the Stage enough:

1. **I am bored with working on it.** I have fiddled and played with it enough that I do not want to keep doing that.
2. **I cannot think of another addition that is both important and interesting for the characters.** Just because something might never be used is no excuse for it to be boring.
3. **It makes sense.** I can understand why everything is there and how each piece affects the others.
4. **I can envision a populated world emerging from it.** It feels like a living portion of the setting, not just a collection of isolated ideas.

The fourth criterion is difficult to explain, especially when the game's existing setting already supplies a populated world. I am not trying to create every person in it. I want the part I have developed to add depth and feel alive within that world.

#### What I Deliberately Leave Undecided ####

Most of what I create for the Stage never sees the light of day. That is a good thing. Material I make without the players' input is never as good as the ideas we generate together.

The Stage gives me a large grab-bag to draw from when I am surprised. I can use something directly or use it to create something new. Its value is not measured by how much of it I manage to show the players. I am building understanding and possibilities, not a list of things they must encounter.

I leave the developing story open. I do not prepare the characters' decisions, a required sequence of events, or an ending the players must reach. The forces and Stage help me respond coherently without needing to predict those things.

##### Arcs and Stories #####

I use "Arc" and "Story" interchangeably. A collision starts an Arc: the events that fall out of that collision belong to the same narrative device. That device can end, even while the campaign continues.

An Arc ends in one of two ways:

- The players stop engaging with it.
- Its fallout reaches a natural conclusion based on character actions.

A natural ending gives the table a sense of having completed something. In rulesets that award experience for completing stories or similar milestones, it also provides a natural point to gain XP.

I suggest having three Arcs in play, introducing them across three sessions rather than starting everything at once. That staggered start lets complexity grow and gives the campaign a sense of depth. It is a rule of thumb, not a schedule I protect from play. I am willing to change it, or anything else, when play calls for that.

The important distinction is that the three Arcs begin with three different collisions involving three different pairs of goals. They are not simply three threads from one collision. As another rule of thumb, I involve no more than two forces in each collision.

The same forces can participate in different Arcs. It is possible for the same pair of forces to collide over different pairs of goals, but I do not suggest that as the starting arrangement.

##### Preparing a Collision #####

Before an Arc starts, I know:

- The two forces involved.
- The goals driving their actions.
- What caused the conflict.
- The combatants.

For the first combat of the game, I also know where it takes place and whether I intend it to be a victory or a defeat for the characters. Otherwise, the location remains undecided. Everything else is open.

For example, consider these three forces:

- **Force A** wants to become mayor.
- **Force B** wants to bring all crime in the city under its control.
- **Force C** wants to remove its biggest business competitor from the city.

None of those goals directly opposes another. The collisions come from what the forces do to pursue them:

1. **A and C collide over a strike.** C has caused a strike, and A uses local authorities to break it up to gain votes in the upcoming election.
2. **B and C collide over a drive-by.** C's beefed-up private security stops a drive-by near its business that would have eliminated a gang leader.
3. **A and B collide through public violence.** A gang leader's daughter works for A. B uses bribed authorities to take out that leader with lethal force at a conference for A.

These can start three distinct Arcs using only three forces.

The conference is an example of where the event might happen, not a place I need to push the characters toward. Before that session, I only need to know that B will oppose A through violence in a public space because the gang leader's daughter works for A. I choose the public space based on where the characters go.

That is how I leave later collisions flexible enough to weave into character actions. I prepare the conflict, not the characters' route to it.

#### How Characters Connect to the Game ####

Usually, I do most of this development after the table has formed but before we meet to make characters. Character creation then gives me details to backfill into the Stage.

There is no fixed amount of information I give the players before character creation. It depends on the theme and the particular game. Knowing the theme, Stage, initial forces, and opening collision gives me material to decide what the players should know and what their characters should know.

I share a detail when it serves one or more of these purposes:

1. It prevents surprise about the type of game being run.
2. It guides players toward characters who fit the Stage and chosen theme.
3. It helps explain the opening combat afterward.

I keep those details as brief as possible, and no briefer. I want enough information for players to make fitting characters and understand the kind of game they are joining, without making them sit through unnecessary opening rhetoric. Content expectations and safety boundaries still need to be established; reducing exposition does not replace that conversation.

Sometimes I do not know the inciting incident until the characters are made. I have even held off on creating the Stage and forces until then. I do not recommend that unless the GM and players are experienced and have played many games together.

#### Giving Players Something Worth Engaging With ####

##### The Opening Collision #####

I always start the game with combat arising from a collision of forces. The characters do not have to fight the forces directly; they can be caught in the fallout of their actions.

Most games have their most developed rules in combat. Starting there lets the players try their new characters using the part of the game the rules support most heavily. It also focuses the table immediately. I have never had an opening combat fail to engage the players; it was the way I found to begin a campaign with everyone interested.

But the opening combat is the dreaded railroad. The characters must already have made some decision to be in a place where the combat can happen. I am making that starting decision for them, so I do not want to build too much around it. This prepared frame is useful only for the first few moments of the first session; once play is underway, I follow the players' choices rather than treating the opening as a route the campaign must continue to follow.

My rule is: **The decision must be something the players can accept that their characters did before the game started.**

If they cannot accept that premise, I have lost their engagement before combat begins. Preparing an opening situation is not permission to assign them choices that do not fit their characters.

##### A Non-Lethal First Fight #####

As a rule of thumb, the opening combat needs to be guaranteed non-lethal. This is the players' first chance to use their characters, and they are going to assume they will win. Winning does not have to happen, but losing should not mean losing those new characters.

I ensure this through the encounter and its consequences rather than announcing the guarantee beforehand. My goal is to reduce opening rhetoric; the players do not need an explanation of this preparation. They need to see the consequences afterward.

When I intend the opening to be a victory, I make the combat well below the characters' abilities: a sure win. When I intend it to be a loss, the opposition's objective is to capture or drive them away, and the enemies do not use lethal combat techniques.

This is a specific decision about the first fight, not a predetermined outcome for the Arc. The characters' responses and the events that follow remain open.

##### Letting Questions Bring Out the Background #####

Once the combat is over, the players start asking questions. Now I can give them the opening explanation because they are seeking it instead of waiting for me to finish talking.

In one campaign, every character had a police officer as a contact. That connection existed before the fight, but afterward I explained that the characters were there because the contact had asked them to look into something. I gave everyone a free advantage because I knew what the opening needed.

The connection made the starting decision plausible for the characters. The combat gave the players something immediate to do. Their questions then gave me a way to explain the situation when they wanted to understand it.

#### Trying This Approach ####

Begin with a theme, a force, or a piece of the setting that interests you. Develop the Stage and forces together until you understand why those forces matter and can envision a living world around them. Do not treat every idea you generate as something that must appear in play.

Look for distinct collisions between the forces' ways of pursuing their goals. Prepare the forces, goals, cause of conflict, and combatants. For the opening, choose a location and an outcome that does not kill the new characters, and make sure the starting premise is something the players can accept.

Give players enough information to make characters who fit, then use their ideas to deepen the Stage. Keep later collisions flexible enough to happen where play takes you. The starting point should give you something to respond with, not something you have to make the players follow.

### 6. Preparing for Play ###

#### What I Prepare and Why ####

Preparing a campaign and preparing for a session are different kinds of work. Before play begins, I spend about 70% of my initial preparation building the Stage and about 20% building the forces. That work gives me an understanding of the world and the people or groups acting in it. It is not a schedule of events for the characters to follow.

Between sessions, I prepare much less. I look at what the characters did and ask what interesting fallout follows from it. I use that fallout as my starting point for the next session. I am not trying to predict what the characters will do next; I am getting ready to respond to what they have already changed.

I prepare the things the characters will need to spend effort on. If there is a clue for them to pursue, I prepare it. If there are combatants for them to defeat, I prepare them. If there is a key character they may try to build a relationship with, I prepare that character. The players decide what to do with these things and what comes of their efforts.

#### What My Notes Look Like ####

People need to find the level of detail and format that work best for them. I keep my notes brief, and I use Markdown for everything. I usually give each important thing its own short file. I try to keep a force to no more than two screens of information, and hope to use less.

The point is not to fit a particular amount of information into a file. The notes should be short enough that I can use them, and detailed enough to help me make decisions. I do not need to write down every possibility. My notes are there to help me understand what is happening and respond when the players take the game somewhere I did not expect.

##### Improvising Without Looking Unprepared #####

Many GMs, especially new ones, worry that improvising will make them look disorganized or unprepared. I understand that fear. The answer is not to plan every scene or plot turn in advance. It is to prepare the parts that let you make sense of what happens: the Stage, the forces and their goals, their relationships, and the consequences already in motion.

That understanding gives you something solid to work from when the players do something unexpected. You can make a new detail fit what is already true, or notice a pattern and decide what in the world could explain it. The players may experience the result as a world that was fully planned, even when you are creating the connection in the moment. That is not a trick to fool them; it is a way to create a shared sense of wonder. Preparation supports the improvisation that makes the moment feel magical and memorable.

#### When Preparation Is Sufficient ####

A session is ready to play when I know what interesting fallout will follow from what happened last session. I also prepare the things that will require effort from the characters, such as clues, combatants, and key NPCs.

This is a practical stopping point, not a promise that I know what the session will contain. The characters may ignore a clue, avoid a fight, or connect with an NPC in a way I did not anticipate. I prepare what they might engage with; I do not prepare the choices they will make or decide in advance how those choices turn out.

#### What I Don't Prepare ####

I do not prepare a required sequence of events, the characters' decisions, or an ending they have to reach. I do not need to decide exactly how the characters will encounter later conflicts. I prepare enough to understand the situation and what may follow from their actions, then leave room for the players to change it.

I also do not try to prepare every possible clue, encounter, or interaction. I prepare the ones that matter to the situation and that call for effort from the characters. The rest can emerge during play, informed by the Stage, the forces, and what has already happened.

#### An Annotated Example of My Session Prep ####

Here is the sort of thing I prepare before a session. The exact format changes from game to game, but the pattern stays the same: I note the fallout from the last session, identify the questions that matter, and prepare the things the characters are likely to spend effort on. I do not write a script. I write a situation.

##### Example: After the warehouse attack #####

The last session ended with the characters exposing a forged permit at the River Market and forcing a confrontation with the guild's private enforcers. The market is furious, frightened, and eager to find someone to blame. The characters are now the obvious target.

```text
Session Prep: River Market

Fallout
- The warehouse fire is still smoldering; people are scared, angry, and looking for a scapegoat.
- The guild is suppressing rumors, but a few workers are willing to talk if the characters can promise safety.
- The spirit beneath the city is stirring and leaving traces in the old drains beneath the market.

Things that require effort
- Clue: a ledger page showing payment to a councilor tied to the guild.
- Clue: a half-burned note reading "salt the shrine before sunrise."
- Combatants: four masked enforcers, two dock thugs, one guild fixer.
- Key NPC: Ilya Moss, a broker who wants the characters to keep the market quiet while she figures out what the guild is hiding.

Open questions
- Does the councilor know what the guild is doing, or is the guild using him?
- Is the spirit reacting to the characters, or just to the disturbances above it?
- What happens if the characters expose the ledger before they can verify it?
```

The value of this prep is not that the notes are complete. They are not. The point is that I have identified the pressure points. The market is unstable. People are willing to talk. There are clues worth following. There are enemies the characters might fight. There is a person with leverage and a reason to talk to them. Those are the ingredients I need to improvise from.

##### Why This Works #####

I write down the fallout that matters, not a timeline of events. The market is angry because of what happened last session, and that anger creates a reason for the next session to begin with tension. I prepare a small set of material things the characters might investigate, take interest in, or use. I prepare the enforcers and the broker because those are the things the characters may need to fight or negotiate with. I leave the details fluid because the players are the ones who decide which questions they ask and what they do with the answers.

The open questions are the real structure. They tell me what is uncertain and what need not be decided yet. If the players ignore the ledger and pursue the shrine, the market still matters because the market itself is full of suspicion and fallout. If they talk to Ilya, she can steer them, threaten them, or offer them a bargain. If they attack the enforcers, the guild responds, and the tension in the city becomes a new problem rather than a pre-written plot beat.

This is the point of prepared session notes for me: they help me understand the pressure in the room, the questions the players might ask, and the likely consequences of their choices. They do not make the session a script. They keep the campaign moving without deciding in advance what the characters will do.

## Part III: Running the Game ##

* [7. My Basic Loop at the Table](#7-my-basic-loop-at-the-table)
* [8. Making Decisions in the Moment](#8-making-decisions-in-the-moment)
* [9. Keeping Play Moving](#9-keeping-play-moving)
* [10. Bringing the World to Life](#10-bringing-the-world-to-life)

### 7. My Basic Loop at the Table ###

#### The Loop ####

At the table, I keep returning to a simple loop: I present what is happening, find out what the players want to do, decide what needs resolution, establish what changes, and give the situation back to them. This is not a script or a set of steps I have to perform mechanically. It is a way to keep play responsive: the players can act on what they see, and the world can change in response.

#### Present What Is Happening ####

I describe the part of the situation the characters can perceive and act on. That might be what a person is doing, what has changed because of an earlier action, or the immediate effects of a force pursuing its goal. I give enough information for the players to understand what their characters could reasonably notice, but I do not need to explain the whole Stage or every cause behind the moment.

If the characters have questions, I answer from what they know, what they can discover, and what is actually true in the world. Sometimes the players' questions are the best cue for what background to explain. I want them to learn about the situation because they are interested in it, not because I have stopped play to deliver everything I prepared.

#### Find Out What the Players Want to Do ####

I let the players decide what their characters attempt. I do not assume they will follow a prepared lead, take a particular side, or respond in the way I expected. If I am unsure what a player means, I ask what the character is trying to accomplish or how they intend to approach it. That gives me a better basis for deciding what happens without taking the choice away from them.

The players' choices can redirect the situation. The forces and the Stage give me material to respond with, but they do not dictate what the characters must do or what the story must become.

#### Decide What Needs Resolution ####

Once I understand the intention, I decide whether anything needs to be resolved. Some actions are clear from the situation and need no roll or extended discussion. When the outcome is uncertain and matters, I use the relevant rules, make a ruling, or talk through the situation with the players. How I choose between those approaches, and how I handle a difficult ruling, belongs to the next chapter.

#### Establish What Changes ####

When resolving a situation, I put on my evil GM's hat. I ask myself: **What are the worst things that could plausibly happen because of this action?** I do not invent danger just to make things harder. I look to what is already in the game: the Stage, the forces and their goals and limits, what the characters know but might be overlooking, and what they do not know yet. A consequence can also hint at something hidden, as long as it grows out of the situation rather than arriving as an arbitrary twist.

Then I prune. I discard consequences that would kill interest, momentum, player agency, or fun. Starting with the worst possibilities helps me notice the stakes; it does not mean I choose the worst one. I want the result to matter without making the players feel that their choices were pointless.

The characters can win and still leave the story open. Their success should stand. A consequence might add a cost, expose a new problem, change a relationship, draw attention, or reveal a danger. It should give the players something meaningful to respond to, not secretly cancel what they accomplished or force them down a predetermined path.

#### Give the Situation Back to the Players ####

I make the change visible, then return the focus to the players. They need to see enough of what happened to choose what their characters do next. That may mean showing the immediate result, describing a reaction, or revealing a clue to a larger problem. I do not need to explain every implication at once; the players can investigate, ask questions, or move in another direction.

Their next choice begins the loop again. The forces react to what the characters have changed, and the world develops from the actions at the table. I use the loop to keep play moving while leaving the outcome open.

### 8. Making Decisions in the Moment ###

#### Choosing How to Resolve Something ####

When a character tries something, I first decide whether the outcome needs resolving at all. If it is clear from the situation, I say what happens and keep play moving. If the outcome is uncertain and matters, I use the rules, make a ruling, or talk it through with the players. I choose the approach that helps us understand what happens without letting the process get in the way of the game.

Rules are useful tools, not authorities that outrank the people playing. If a rule supports the moment, I use it. If I do not know the rule, I let the player attempt the action for now and tell them I will check it for future sessions. If the dice or system are getting in the way of the table's fun, I set them aside and play make-believe instead.

#### Handling Uncertainty and Missing Information ####

I do not need to know everything before making a decision. I use what is established: the Stage, the forces and their goals and limits, what the characters know, and what has already happened. If something important is unclear, I can ask the players what they mean, talk through the uncertainty, or make a provisional ruling so play can continue.

When I have to fill a gap, I want the answer to belong to the world we have established. I do not treat uncertainty as permission to invent a consequence that has no connection to the situation. If I later discover that I misunderstood a rule or a fact, I can correct how I handle it from then on without erasing the events that have already happened.

#### Making Rulings Players Can Understand ####

I try to make rulings in terms of the character and the situation, and to say enough that the players understand what I am deciding. I do not need to turn every call into a long debate. My usual framework is:

1. **I do not know the rule:** The player can do it for now. I will look up the rule before a future session.
2. **The character probably cannot do it, but the attempt is plausible:** I may allow it with a slight increase in difficulty.
3. **The action is too outlandish for the character:** I use “No, but.” I say no to that specific action, then help the player find another way to pursue the character's goal.

If there is a conflict about a rule or ruling, I bring it to a table vote and move on. Safety is different: any player can veto content without explanation, and that veto is not put to a vote.

#### Consistency Without Being Trapped by Precedent ####

I want events to fit the players' view of the world because that helps them trust it. Literal consistency is less important than that appearance: a new explanation or detail can be worked in afterward if it does not break what the players understand to be true. Players often help make those connections themselves. This is separate from rules precedent. Sometimes I make a call in the moment and later learn that the rules do not support it. What happened, happened. The character did the thing, and the consequences remain part of the game. It was a fluke; the same action is not necessarily possible again.

I explain the correction and apply the rules or ruling consistently going forward. I do not take back a past success just to make the record match the rulebook. This lets me correct course without making the players feel that their earlier choices or accomplishments can be retroactively invalidated.

#### Correcting a Decision That Did Not Work ####

If a decision is making play less fun, undermining a character, or creating a problem I did not intend, I can acknowledge that and change how I handle things. I do not have to defend a bad call just because I made it. I explain what I am changing, preserve what has already happened where I can, and move forward with a clearer understanding.

There is one exception to leaving past events in place. If an action causes someone to raise a safety concern, that action is erased, along with its direct consequences. Safety overrides continuity, rules, and the desire to preserve what happened. I make a note of the concern without asking for an explanation, then help the affected player find another way forward if the action was theirs.

### 9. Keeping Play Moving ###

#### Recognizing What Deserves Attention ####

I pay attention to what the players respond to. What they ask about, pursue, and keep engaging with tells me what is interesting to them. I do not give every prepared idea equal time just because I prepared it. If the players chase other Arcs, I let a less-attended Arc languish, even while its events continue in the background and its consequences remain visible. I do not treat that as a reason to force the Arc forward or resolve it for them.

An Arc losing the players' attention is different from a player losing interest in the game. If I am concerned about a player's engagement—for example, if they start spending time on their phone—I talk with them privately after the session rather than treating it as a story problem. If someone says directly that they do not like a thread, I take that seriously. Preparation gives me possibilities, not an obligation to keep presenting material the players do not want.

#### Giving Players Room Without Losing Momentum ####

I do not try to maintain momentum by filling every pause or pushing the players toward a decision. I let them think, talk, ask questions, and decide what matters to their characters. Awkward silence can be useful. It gives a player space to work out what they want to do, and I may remind the rest of the table to let that space exist rather than rushing to fill it.

For me, momentum comes from the situation changing in response to the players, not from hurrying them. When they are ready to act, the forces and the Stage give me material for a response. If a thread stops holding their interest, I can follow their attention elsewhere instead of forcing it forward.

#### Sharing Attention Among Players ####

I avoid asking the table a broad question like, “What are you all doing now?” Instead, I address each player through their character. After a conflict, for example, I might ask, “What is Luna thinking? What is your next priority?” This gives each player a direct opening to contribute without requiring them to compete for space in a group conversation.

After I have heard from each player, I ask the table to make a plan together. I give them a few moments to talk, then go around and check in with each player again, still using their character's name. The group has room to collaborate, while each person still gets a chance to say what their character wants.

I do not have a complete formula for sharing attention. It is nuanced and changes with the people and situation at the table. This is one technique I use to make sure that everyone has an invitation to take part.

#### Handling Hesitation and Unexpected Choices ####

When a player hesitates, I do not assume that the pause means something has gone wrong. I can leave room for them to think rather than immediately supplying an answer or choosing a direction for them. The other players can help by respecting that pause.

When players make an unexpected choice, I follow it. I do not steer them back toward the path I expected or treat an unused prepared thread as a failure. Their choice changes the situation; I use what I know about the Stage and forces to respond.

#### Knowing When to Move On ####

I move on from a thread when the players stop engaging with it, or when its fallout reaches a natural conclusion through their actions. I do not keep a force or situation active solely because I prepared it. If the players have lost interest, I can let the thread change, fade, or resolve in whatever way seems most interesting, then give attention to what the table wants to explore.

Moving on does not mean the world has to forget what happened. A thread may leave consequences behind even after it stops taking focus. I keep the parts that matter to the developing situation and let the rest go.

### 10. Bringing the World to Life ###

#### Deciding What to Describe ####

I try to give at least two concrete details for each scene and for every NPC or group of NPCs. I describe enough of the background for people to understand the situation, then let their minds fill in the rest. The details do not need to be elaborate. They need to give the players something specific to picture and act on.

For example:

> As you wait in the dimly lit parking lot of a medium-sized church, three rough-looking men ride up on Harley-Davidson motorcycles. They are the remaining heads of the local gangs, and they look pissed.

That is the whole lead-up description. The parking lot and church establish the scene; the men, their motorcycles, and their anger make the arrival concrete. The players know who has arrived and what kind of moment this is without needing a long description of the lot, the building, or each man's appearance. I give them enough to imagine the scene, then leave space for their own picture of it.

#### Portraying People and Their Motivations ####

I want NPCs to feel like people with reasons for what they do, not pieces I move around to deliver information or serve a plot. Every NPC has goals. Those goals are often immediate and obvious, and they govern the NPC's actions and interactions with the characters.

An NPC can still serve a purpose in the campaign. In one game, I had a woman who was meant to give the players information and demonstrate one of the forces' power. She was also trying to save her son, who was a prisoner of war. If she succeeded, he would live free; if she failed, he would remain a POW. That goal shaped every interaction she had with the characters. Her campaign role did not replace her own reason to act.

NPCs also have emotions. Most of the time, these are not explosive or theatrical, but they still affect how people respond. If the characters insult an NPC, that person might act injured or self-righteous, depending on who they are and what they want. The goal gives the interaction direction; the emotion gives it a human texture.

In combat, I make sure at least one NPC has a name and is called by it. A name gives the fight weight and draws attention to the fact that these are people. If I have the time and inspiration while preparing, I name all the combatants.

#### Responding to What the Characters Do ####

The characters' significant actions change the situation. I do not decide in advance what those actions must lead to; I look at what follows from what the characters actually did and from the people, forces, and relationships already in the game.

I expect every significant act to have at least two consequences, and sometimes more. I do this to help the players feel that their characters matter: their actions can keep changing the world beyond the moment in which they happened. One consequence is usually fairly immediate; another may surface several sessions later as the wider situation adjusts. These consequences do not have to balance each other or make every success costly. They can point in different directions, or they can all be beneficial or harmful. They are not a way to take back a success or punish the characters for acting. They let the world respond to what the characters have done.

If the characters kill the head of a local gang, the people that person hurt may thank them. At the same time, removing that leader can destabilize the underground power structure and increase gang violence. Both results follow from the same act. The characters accomplished something real, and the situation has changed in ways they may now have to deal with.

#### Making Consequences Visible ####

I want the players to encounter the effects of their choices, even when those effects are not immediately obvious. Consequences do not have to arrive as an NPC explaining what the characters caused. They can show up in changed circumstances, other people's behavior, or details of ordinary life.

In one game, the characters were trying to find the cause of a massacre that had happened twenty years earlier. In doing so, they accidentally started a real-estate war. Land prices soared and housing costs rose so sharply that the news began reporting on apartments where large numbers of people were sharing rooms.

That kind of ripple makes the characters important even if the world does not know why things are happening. The people in those apartments do not need to know that the characters' investigation helped cause the changes. The characters' actions still reach beyond the people they meet directly, and a news report can make that larger effect visible without stopping to explain every link in the chain. The realization that an action from two games ago helped drive up housing costs can give the players a sense of awe at their characters' reach. In another game, stopping an evil corporation meant that its factory site eventually became a park. A consequence can be a lasting improvement, not just a new problem.

#### Keeping the World Coherent as It Changes ####

The world can change in ways I did not plan, but I want those changes to grow out of what is already happening. I use the Stage, the forces' goals and limits, their relationships, and the actions people have taken to work out what might follow. That gives me a basis for improvising without having to predict the characters' choices.

Sometimes a consequence will be indirect or take time to appear. I do not need to reveal the whole chain at once. I can let the players see a new effect first, then discover its connection as they ask questions or investigate. The characters may never learn every connection, and the wider world may never recognize their part in what changed.

The point is not to make the world react to every choice in a way that announces, “This was because of you.” It is to let the characters' choices matter. The world can respond, adapt, and keep moving around them, whether or not anyone understands why.

I rarely need to plan a surprise. Logical fallout can surprise the players because I know more about the Stage, forces, and relationships than they do. A consequence that seems obvious to me may be unexpected to them; the difference in what we know lets ordinary cause and effect produce surprising revelations without a planned twist.

## Part IV: Beyond a Single Session ##

* [11. Ending a Session and Starting the Next](#11-ending-a-session-and-starting-the-next)
* [12. Letting a Campaign Develop](#12-letting-a-campaign-develop)

### 11. Ending a Session and Starting the Next ###

#### Finding a Stopping Point ####

Most of my games are timebound. We agree when we start when the session will end, and I plan to respect that time. My hard rule is not to end while the characters are in the middle of doing something. I look for a point between activities: before or after combat, a political scene, an intrigue, or an investigation.

I love cliffhangers, but I do not plan for them or try to encourage them. If a good one happens naturally, I am often willing to end a few minutes early or late to use it. I will not stretch the session by more than about fifteen minutes for that. A cliffhanger is a welcome stopping point, not a reason to push the players toward one or disregard the time we agreed on.

#### What I Record Afterward ####

After a session, I keep simple notes. I record what the players did in general terms, then note the significant things the characters did specifically. I also record what affected each force, what affected the Stage, and what rewards the characters earned, including XP and other rewards.

I do not need a transcript of the session. I want to preserve what changed and what is likely to matter again. Those notes help me remember the characters' actions and keep track of how the world has responded to them.

#### What I Ask the Players ####

After every session, I ask the players, “How could this be better?” I listen and record their advice, but I do not take each suggestion at face value or immediately treat it as an instruction to change something.

I compare feedback across sessions and look for patterns. If I start to see one, I open a session with a discussion about it. I want to understand why the players are making those suggestions. The reason behind the feedback matters more to me than the particular fix someone proposes. Once I understand what is not working for them, we can talk about what would address it.

#### Turning the Session into Useful Preparation ####

The things I record are also the material I use to prepare for the next session. What the players did, which character actions mattered, what those actions changed in the forces or the Stage, and what rewards they earned all help me decide what is worth carrying forward. I look at what happened and ask what interesting fallout might follow. I prepare to respond to the changed situation, not to predict what the characters will do next.

The first four sessions are an exception. At that point, the characters may have done too little to propel the campaign and create much fallout of their own. I pay close attention to what has engaged the players and use those apparent interests to create inciting incidents that may appeal to them. As the characters' actions begin to change the situation, those actions and their effects become the main material feeding into the next session.

### 12. Letting a Campaign Develop ###

#### What Persists Between Sessions ####

The campaign carries forward what the characters have done and what those actions have changed. I record their significant actions, what affected each force, what affected the Stage, and what rewards they earned. Those notes are not a plan for what must happen next. They are the current state of the campaign: material I can use to understand the situation and respond.

Forces continue pursuing their goals, within the lines they will and will not cross. Their goals, resources, and other defining qualities can change as play develops. The Stage changes too. An action may affect people or parts of the world the characters never intended to reach, and those effects can become part of what the campaign is about.

#### Following Player Interests ####

I pay attention to what the players choose to engage with. Their questions, actions, and continued interest tell me which parts of the campaign matter to them. I follow that attention instead of insisting that they pursue every force, clue, or situation I prepared.

This does not mean the world stops when the characters look elsewhere. Forces can keep pursuing their goals, and situations can change without the characters' involvement. But I do not keep presenting a thread just because I prepared it. If the players disengage, I let it rest, change, or resolve in whatever way seems most interesting. What matters is responding to the table, not protecting my unused plans.

#### Revisiting Unresolved Situations ####

An unresolved situation can remain part of the campaign. If it still matters to the characters or the world, it may return or continue to develop. Its return should come from the situation and the characters' actions, not from a requirement to finish everything that has been introduced.

I distinguish between a thread that is complete and one the players have disengaged from. An Arc can end because its fallout reaches a natural conclusion through the characters' actions, or because the players stop engaging with it. Both are ways to move on during play, but they are not the same kind of ending. A disengaged thread is not a completed one, and I do not count it as closure when I consider how to end the campaign.

An Arc can end while the campaign continues. New situations can grow from what the characters have done, and active forces can remain or change. The campaign does not need to conclude every unresolved story along the way.

#### Changing Direction ####

I do not decide in advance what the campaign has to become. The characters' choices can redirect it, change forces, alter the Stage, or make an earlier expectation irrelevant. I use what has happened and what the players care about to decide what follows. My preparation helps me improvise within a coherent world; it is not a route back to the story I first imagined.

The campaign's direction can emerge from connections I did not plan. A force may turn out to matter across several stories. A character's action may set off changes far beyond the immediate situation. I let those developments reshape what the campaign is about, while preserving enough continuity for the changes to feel earned.

#### Recognizing When a Campaign Should End ####

A campaign can outlive itself. It is important to end it deliberately instead of letting it simply die from neglect or lost momentum. The campaigns that end are the ones people continue to talk about; the ones that just die tend to disappear from memory.

I look for a point where enough completed threads can connect to the current ones. When one or more active threads reach their end, those connections can make the ending feel satisfying. The skill is finding the right moment to draw things together neatly, but not completely. There should still be loose ends, while the characters have clearly accomplished something major. For me, that ending is usually bittersweet.

In one game, the players discovered that a wizard they had thought was their friend was actually an evil force. He had been active across a good number of their stories. The players fought and defeated him. He was one of three forces in the campaign, but his defeat was the point where I called the campaign over. It surprised the whole table, and they still talk about that ending when they get together.

I had not waited for every thread or force to be resolved. That moment connected the wizard to what the players had experienced, gave them a major accomplishment, and felt like a place to stop. Ending the campaign did not mean explaining or tying off everything. It meant recognizing that the story had reached an ending worth remembering.

## Part V: Learning the Approach ##

* [13. When It Isn't Working](#13-when-it-isnt-working)
* [14. My Approach in Practice](#14-my-approach-in-practice)
* [15. Making This Style Your Own](#15-making-this-style-your-own)

### 13. When It Isn't Working ###

#### Signs the Game Isn't Producing the Intended Experience ####

I want the game to leave people energized, engaged, and still thinking about what happened. A session does not have to follow my plans to succeed, but I pay attention when the players and I are not enjoying the game, or when the play at the table is not producing the experience we agreed to pursue.

One quiet session is not enough to diagnose a problem. A player may be thinking, tired, or simply less interested in a particular thread. A thread losing the players' attention is not the same as a player losing interest in the game. I look for patterns in how people respond, and I ask the players how the game could be better. Their feedback helps me notice a problem, but I still need to understand what is behind it before choosing a change.

Sometimes the problem is local. A ruling, encounter, or scene may be slowing play down or making a character feel ineffective. Sometimes the players are engaged with the campaign, but not with the material I expected them to care about. And sometimes the group wants a different kind of game from the one I want to run. Those are different problems; they need different responses.

#### Distinguishing a Technique Problem from a Mismatch ####

When something is not working, I try to determine whether the game needs a different technique or whether we want different experiences. I can change how I present a situation, follow a different thread, or let go of a prepared idea. But I cannot make a genuine mismatch disappear by pushing the players toward my preferred style.

The first time I ran Fate Core, the players made characters and chose concepts that did not fit the kind of game I like to run. After two sessions, neither the players nor I were having fun. I could not see a way to add the elements I wanted without invalidating their choices, so I ended the campaign.

That was not a problem I could solve by steering the characters toward my plans. Doing that would have asked the players to give up the characters they had chosen in order to make the game suit me. Ending the campaign was better than continuing to run a game that was not working for any of us.

The next time I ran Fate Core, I was clearer about the style of game I wanted and developed the Stage before character creation. That gave the players useful material for making characters who could find fun in a genre I would enjoy running too. I had changed what I could control—how I explained the game and how much context I prepared—rather than trying to change the players' choices after the fact.

#### What to Adjust First ####

Before changing the campaign, I listen for what the players are actually responding to. I ask what could be better, consider the reasons behind their suggestions, and look for patterns rather than treating every comment as an instruction to follow literally. I also take my own enjoyment seriously. I am part of the table, and a game that consistently makes the GM unhappy is not a sustainable success.

If the players are engaged but a particular part is not working, I can change that part. I can spend less time on a thread they are not pursuing, make a ruling differently, or prepare a clearer situation for the next session. I do not need to preserve an idea just because I spent time preparing it. The Stage and forces exist to help me respond to play, not to compete with it.

In one campaign, I had prepared an evil wizard who had been corrupting the city for decades, a Vampire Lord who controlled its largest businesses, and a tribe of weregators trying to gain control of the city government for spiritual reasons. The players found the parts of the Stage connected to the wizard much more interesting than the weregators. They began investigating what had happened decades before the game started.

I followed that interest. The campaign became more of a “True Crime” story, and I developed Time as a force: the past appeared through reflections, and Time's goal was retribution for a single sin the wizard had committed. I had not planned for the past to become so important, and Time was not a force I had imagined before play. The players' interest showed me what in the Stage was worth developing.

That was not a case of rescuing a failing campaign by making the players return to the weregators. The game was giving us a direction that interested the players, and my preparation let me build on it. I could let an unused part recede and turn a detail the players cared about into something with agency and consequences.

#### Repairing Mistakes with the Group ####

Sometimes the problem comes from a decision I made. If a ruling or technique is making play less fun, undermining a character, or producing a consequence I did not intend, I can acknowledge that and change how I handle it. I explain what I am changing, preserve what has already happened where I can, and apply the new understanding consistently from then on.

Repair does not mean pretending the problem did not happen. I want to understand what went wrong and what would help the group move forward. A conversation may clarify that I misunderstood what the players wanted, that a technique did not work for them, or that we had different expectations from the start.

Safety is different from ordinary game problems. A player can veto content without explanation, and the offending context and its direct consequences are removed. I do not ask the group to weigh that against continuity, preparation, or anyone's preferred story.

#### When a Different Approach Is Better ####

If the players and I want different kinds of games, we can talk about whether there is an experience we would all enjoy. I can change what I run, the group can choose a different game, or we can decide not to continue together. But if the only way to make the campaign work is to invalidate player choices or make someone at the table keep playing a game they do not enjoy, it may be time to stop.

Ending a campaign is not proof that the GM failed. Sometimes it is the clearest way to respect what the people at the table want. In my first Fate Core campaign, I ended the game when I could not see a way to bring my preferred elements in without taking away the players' choices. The next time, I explained the kind of game I wanted up front and built a Stage that could help everyone find a place in it.

When something is not working, I try to find out what the experience is telling me. If the players are showing me what interests them, I follow that interest. If I have made a mistake, I own it and repair what I can. If our expectations do not fit, I say so rather than forcing the game to continue. The aim is not to save every campaign or every idea; it is to make a game the people at the table can enjoy together.

### 14. My Approach in Practice ###

This example follows a Mage: The Ascension 20th Anniversary Edition campaign with multiple supernatural crossovers, set in modern Baton Rouge. It shows how I reuse ideas, develop a Stage, choose starting forces, and then follow the players when their interests take the campaign somewhere I had not planned.

#### Reusing an Earlier Idea ####

Before this campaign, I had developed another game around a hidden Nephandi, a spirit beneath the city, and the idea of Time becoming a force. That campaign fell through for reasons unrelated to the game. I liked much of what had happened in the preparation and play, though, so I used it as inspiration rather than abandoning the material.

I did not carry over a finished plot. I took pieces that interested me and built a new Stage around them. Some details came from Baton Rouge itself. The city is known as Red Stick because, according to local history, settlers found the area marked by sticks with red tops, placed there by Native people. No one knows what the sticks meant or why they were there.

In my Stage, the Mokolé had placed the sticks to mark the resting place of a minor reptile Incarna. That gave the real-world mystery a supernatural history and connected the land to a group whose present-day interests could grow from it.

#### Building the Stage Through Its History ####

I gave Baton Rouge a recent supernatural history that shaped the city before the characters arrived. Cane awoke for twenty-four hours and followed Cane's law, killing the worst offenders he encountered. At the time, Johnathan Harker, a young Euthanatos protégé who was blood bound to the Prince, used his contacts to form an army intended to kill Cane. They failed. In the aftermath, the vampires, mages, and werewolves in Baton Rouge were dead.

One werewolf survived: Johnathan's best friend, a Ronin Glass Walker whose tribal name was Jester. Jester had been unable to convince anyone that the attack was futile, so he ran. Around the same time, a Rokea who had been living on land fled at the thought that Cane was coming to town. She was careless, captured by her own kind, and killed. Shortly after these events, the Avatar Storm happened.

Johnathan had also been taken under the wing of a respected Celestial Chorister. The Chorister was secretly a Nephandi, and Johnathan was on his way to becoming one too, though he did not know it. These connections meant that the city's past contained both a public catastrophe for its supernatural population and a hidden personal history that could still affect the present.

The Mokolé's mark in the landscape also mattered in modern Baton Rouge. With other supernatural creatures absent for more than twenty years, the Mokolé were trying to buy as much land as possible. Their aim was to have the federal government declare Baton Rouge tribal lands. The same history that explained the sticks therefore created a present-day political goal.

At first, I had focused too much on supernatural events. I realized that the disappearance of the city's supernatural population should also have natural, visible consequences. Without vampires controlling the underworld, it had grown rich and diverse. Control of that underworld had become desirable, and a gang war was underway. The mayor was campaigning on a “War Against Crime” platform.

Adding these consequences gave the Stage more than supernatural mysteries. It created everyday pressures, public politics, and criminal conflict that could affect the characters whether or not they knew the supernatural history behind them. The change also gave me more possibilities for forces: individual gang leaders and the mayor could each have become forces, alongside the Mokolé and supernatural actors.

#### Choosing the Starting Forces ####

I consolidated the gangs into one force. They were not a single organization, but together they were trying to control Baton Rouge. Their fingerprint was disorganization and internal conflict: their actions showed the instability of several groups acting toward a shared goal without being unified.

The Nephandi was another starting force. He was likable and charismatic, and obsessively careful not to be discovered. His fingerprint was the lack of a fingerprint: when he acted, there was a strange void around who or what had caused it. His goal was to corrupt the Incarna and then kill it, creating a Nexus of corruption in the heart of Baton Rouge.

My third starting force was Time, carried forward from the earlier game's ideas. Time wanted to free Jester from survivor's guilt. The Mokolé and the mayor remained part of the Stage, but I did not make them part of the starting trio. I had a populated situation with more possible actors than I needed to make active forces at once.

#### Starting with a Collision ####

The inciting incident came from a collision between the gangs and the Nephandi. The gangs were disposing of evidence near one of his corruption sites. If they continued, they might draw attention to what he was doing to the spirit. He arranged for them to fight, and the conflict became a shootout in a Taco Bell where the characters were having lunch.

The characters were caught in the fallout of actions they had not caused and did not yet understand. The opening did not require them to know about the Incarna, the Nephandi, or the gang's evidence. The collision gave them an immediate situation to respond to, while the reasons behind it could emerge through play.

#### Following the Players into the Gang War ####

The players focused on the gangs. I had used conflicts with them to show their brutality, but in each case a gang leader did something that angered a player. The players used their creativity and Magick to kill that leader. Then another gang leader died in a similar way.

Those deaths were not planned by me. They were consequences of what the players chose to do. After the second, though, the pattern felt too coincidental to leave unexplained. I added a fourth force: a hit man hired to destabilize the gangs.

The hit man's fingerprint was a method rather than a calling card. He, she, or it arranged situations so that someone else had a reason to kill the intended target. The gang leaders' deaths remained the players' actions; the new force gave the repeated pattern a cause inside the world without taking those choices away from them.

This is where fast thinking and improvisation paid off. In one scene, the characters worked with a security guard who gave them information. Later, I put the same person in the background as a janitor cowering in the corner. I used that moment to let the characters recognize him and to establish a second fingerprint for the hit man: he was always present. It was a sudden way to introduce the new force, and the players began looking for him in later scenes. Eventually, he offered them his services. Later, the characters captured him. By then, they were powerful enough that he was no longer a force.

The janitor reveal made the new force feel as if he had been woven through the campaign all along, even though I had only just decided what the pattern meant. That is the kind of moment I want this style of preparation and improvisation to make possible: the players experience a solid, connected world, and the connection arrives as a surprise we can enjoy together.

#### Letting New Forces Emerge ####

The hit man had been hired by a force I had not created at the campaign's start: a cartel daughter who wanted to destabilize the gangs so she could take over their members and build one super gang. The players discovered her under the moniker “Chekhov's Gun.” The name amused me because of how she had come to exist: I had introduced the hit man to explain a pattern created by the players' choices, and that in turn led to the person who had hired him.

The players eventually joined Chekhov's Gun. They thought she was crazy, but she was one of only two people they believed they could trust. The other was the Nephandi. That was surprising to me. I knew what his hidden goal was, but the players judged trust from their characters' experiences and made their own choice.

I did not discourage them from killing gang leaders, steer them toward another force, or try to make them distrust the people they chose to trust. I followed their interest and leaned into it—a “yes, and” approach. When the same kind of death happened again, I asked what might make sense in the world. The answer added depth without undoing what the players had done. Their interest in the gang conflict led to a hit man, the hit man led to Chekhov's Gun, and the characters' own judgments led them to ally with her.

#### What This Example Shows Me ####

The campaign did not unfold from a plot I had prepared. The Stage gave me history, relationships, pressures, and possible forces to draw on. The starting forces created a collision, but the players' choices determined which part of the situation became central. I adjusted the Stage when I saw a gap in it, and I added forces when events at the table made them useful.

The gang leaders were not meant to die as part of a sequence. Their deaths mattered because the players caused them. The hit man did not replace that agency; he helped explain why the situation had begun to feel patterned. Chekhov's Gun gave the hit man's actions a larger purpose, and the players decided what relationship they wanted with her.

For me, the success of this approach was not that I anticipated every turn. I did not. It was that I had enough of a world to build on what the players found interesting, and enough trust in their choices to follow rather than redirect them. The result felt deeper because the campaign's connections grew in response to play, not because I had secretly planned them all in advance.

### 15. Making This Style Your Own ###

You do not need to run games exactly as I do. Some parts of this approach are important to how it works; others are my preferences and rules of thumb. The goal is to understand what each part is doing so you can adapt it to your group and still get the kind of play you want.

#### What Is Essential to the Approach ####

The foundation is to prepare a situation that can respond to the characters. The Stage gives actions context and depth. Forces create movement within it. The characters act on that situation, and their actions change it. Those parts work through their relationships; taking one piece on its own is not the same as trying a smaller version of the approach.

The Stage is especially important. Forces can pursue goals and create conflict, but without a Stage there is little for their movement to mean or connect to. The Stage does not need to cover an entire setting or campaign. It does need to be developed enough to give the characters a place to explore, details to encounter, and relationships or pressures that can produce consequences.

Safety and player agency are not optional techniques to scale down or set aside. Players must be able to make meaningful choices, and safety boundaries take priority over preparation, continuity, and the story. Within those boundaries, you can adapt the rest to your table.

#### Build a Small but Complete System ####

Starting small does not mean using only one force, or preparing a force without a Stage around it. It means building a smaller system with enough connected parts to work. You might focus on one city, one neighborhood, or one part of a larger campaign. Develop that portion of the Stage so the characters can explore it and so the forces' actions have context there.

Put details from the Stage into conversations, places, and rumors. You do not need to explain everything up front. Let the players encounter the material, notice what interests them, and show you where they want to look more closely. Then develop forces in relation to the Stage and to that interest.

I often start by thinking about forces because their goals help me discover what the Stage needs. That is my way into the work, not a requirement that forces come first or matter more. The Stage and forces develop together. What matters is that the result is a functioning whole: a place with depth, forces with reasons to act, and room for the characters' actions to change what happens.

#### Try a Short Shot ####

You can also experiment by running a short campaign rather than planning a long-running one. I call a game intended to last five or fewer sessions a “Short Shot.” A short campaign benefits from a driving goal that gives the limited run direction. It will not be as free-form as a long campaign, and that can be fine given the short time available.

A driving goal gives the group something to engage with; it does not decide how the characters pursue it or require a particular outcome. Keep player agency and safety intact. The campaign can be focused without turning into a script.

For a Short Shot, I have found it useful to provide the players with starting characters and let them put whatever personality they want into them. Character creation can be a lot of effort for a game that will only last a few sessions. Pre-made characters can also make it easier to begin with a group that can work together for the short campaign.

That is a rule of thumb, not a rule. Your players may enjoy making characters, or may already have a cohesive group concept that fits the game. Choose the approach that serves the people at your table.

#### How to Tell Whether It Is Working ####

As you try an adaptation, pay attention to what happens at the table. Do the players find things in the Stage they want to explore? Do their actions change the situation? Can you respond to their choices using what you prepared, without having to force them toward a planned sequence? Are you and the players enjoying the game?

If the area feels empty, add depth to the Stage: relationships, history, people, or pressures that make the place feel inhabited and give actions consequences. If the players are interested in something you did not expect, follow that interest and see how it changes the situation. If the approach is not producing a game your group enjoys, talk about what is missing and adjust—or decide that a different style is a better fit.

You do not need to copy my campaign structure, preparation ratios, opening combat, or number of forces to use the underlying idea. Start with a complete but bounded system, observe what play brings out, and adapt from there. The point is not to reproduce my habits; it is to build a way of preparing and improvising that helps your table create a game worth remembering.
